cards.b:
Pluralists say power in a democracy is spread among many groups: unions, businesses, farmers, religious bodies and NGOs. No single group or class dominates.

The state is like an arena or a referee where these groups compete and bargain.

Early 20th-century British thinkers like Harold Laski, F.W. Maitland and J.N. Figgis attacked the idea of an all-powerful sovereign state.

They argued that churches, guilds and unions have their own real life and authority. The state is just one association among many. Laski even said that because sovereignty is not absolute, it would be good for political science if the concept were given up.

Dahl studied New Haven, Connecticut in Who Governs? (1961). He asked: who really makes decisions here?

He found that different groups won on different issues, such as education, urban renewal and party nominations. No single elite controlled everything. This is polyarchy, rule by many.

In Polyarchy (1971), Dahl said no real country is a perfect democracy. So he used "polyarchy" for real-world democracies.

A polyarchy has two dimensions: public contestation (open competition) and inclusiveness (the right to participate).

Its institutions include elected officials, free and fair elections, universal adult franchise, freedom of expression, alternative sources of information and freedom to form associations.

C. Wright Mills: The Power Elite (1956)

A small group from business, the military and politics really runs the USA.

Bachrach and Baratz: "Two Faces of Power" (1962)

Dahl only saw open decisions. Real power also lies in non-decision making: keeping some issues off the agenda entirely.

Steven Lukes: Power: A Radical View (1974)

A third face: shaping what people even want.

Later pluralists admitted that groups are not equal. In Politics and Markets (1977), Charles Lindblom argued that business holds a privileged position.

Governments depend on business for jobs and growth, so they listen more to business than to anyone else. Dahl himself later accepted that economic inequality distorts democracy.

cards.h: Groups, cross-cutting ties and polyarchy in practice
cards.b:
Pluralists built their theory on studies of interest groups.

  • Arthur Bentley, in The Process of Government (1908), said politics is nothing but the pressure of groups on one another.
  • David Truman, in The Governmental Process (1951), added the idea of overlapping membership. A person can be a worker, a Catholic and a parent at once, so groups cannot become too extreme.
  • Truman also spoke of potential groups: when an interest is threatened, people organise. This keeps the system balanced.

The upshot is a state that acts like a weather vane or broker, responding to whichever group pressures are strongest.

Critics say this is too rosy. E.E. Schattschneider famously wrote that the flaw in the pluralist heaven is that the heavenly chorus sings with a strong upper-class accent.

India looks pluralist in many ways: farmer lobbies, caste associations, trade unions and industry bodies like FICCI and CII all press the government.

Rudolph and Rudolph, in In Pursuit of Lakshmi (1987), called Indian pluralism "involuted pluralism". Many groups are fragmented and weak, while the state remains a strong "third actor". The farm laws protests of 2020–21, which led to the repeal of the laws, show group pressure working.

"Neo-pluralism is a self-critique of pluralism." Comment.

Structure: early pluralism (Laski), American pluralism (Dahl), the elite critique (Mills, Bachrach and Baratz), then neo-pluralism (Lindblom). End with India's involuted pluralism.

quiz.q: The 'privileged position of business' idea comes from…

quiz.w: Bachrach and Baratz, 'Two Faces of Power' (1962).
Rudolph and Rudolph used it for India in In Pursuit of Lakshmi (1987).

quiz.q: The Process of Government (1908) was written by…
Truman's idea that people belong to many groups is called…
'The heavenly chorus sings with a strong upper-class accent' is by…
Early British pluralists like Laski opposed…
quiz.w: They attacked the idea of one absolute sovereign.
Unorganised interests that mobilise when threatened, keeping balance.
